title: 1MW No. 327: The Hidden Cost of Getting Things Done
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this 1-Minute Wednesday, Greg McKeown warns that the habits that make high achievers effective can quietly make them worse company. Essentialism asks us to protect time, cut interruptions and make hard trade-offs, but if we get too good at it we leave no margin and begin to treat the people around us as obstacles. He gives everyday examples such as finishing a colleague's sentences, half-listening to a spouse, or feeling irritated when a child wants to talk as we leave. He cites a 2024 series of five studies with 1,332 participants showing that feeling short on time makes people more goal-focused and more likely to see others as helping or hindering. His conclusion is that margin lets us change plans when something more essential, usually a person, shows up. The action step is to remove one nonessential commitment from the calendar without replacing it and notice how you respond to others.
points: Effectiveness practices such as protecting time can backfire into treating people as interruptions when no margin remains.
Research on time scarcity found it narrows focus on personal goals, even among close friends and naturally helpful people.
Margin is what allows a leader to change plans when something or someone more essential appears.
People are inconveniently unschedulable, and the wisest use of ten minutes may have nothing to do with the plan.
The weekly practice is to cut one nonessential commitment without refilling the space and observe the effect on how you treat others.
quotes: Your priorities should make you more present, not less human. Leave enough margin to remain kind.
But what happens when we get so good at doing these things that we leave no margin in our lives?
But when every minute is spoken for, even someone we love can begin to feel like they're taking something away.

In a 2024 series of five studies involving 1,332 people, researchers found that feeling short on time made people more focused on their own goals and more likely to see others in terms of whether they were helping or getting in the way.
We don't have to stop caring about someone to start treating them like an interruption.
Margin gives us enough room to change our plans when something more essential shows up.
The point of eliminating the nonessential is to become more available for what, and, more importantly, who, is essential.
